Spiking attractor networks are fascinating: they suggest how brains are able to (1) act stably, (2) integrate information distributed across neurons, (3) recover memories etc. despite being composed of billions of seemingly cacophonous neurons. A biologically plausible classifier can be built by fusing two well-supported neural mechanisms: sparse, competitively allocated engram ensembles that store individual experiences, and hierarchical predictive-coding circuits that infer the causes of sensory input through iterative error minimization. Call this architecture the Engram-Predictive Coding Network: a two-module system in which a fast, Hopfield-like engram store interacts with a slower, hierarchical generative-model classifier. The classifier backbone follows the Rao-Ballard scheme, in which each layer holds an estimate of hidden causes r, top-down synaptic weights U encode a generative model predicting the layer below, and inference amounts to maximum-a-posteriori estimation of r from the prediction error between actual and predicted input. Because this scheme uses purely local error signals rather than globally backpropagated derivatives, it satisfies the core biological constraint that action potentials do not travel backward along axons. Salvatori et al. show that a predictive-coding variant, zero-divergence inference learning, generalizes to arbitrary computation graphs and reproduces the exact weight updates of backpropagation using only local, parallel rules, so the hierarchy's output layer can serve as a class-label readout without sacrificing biological realism. The memory module is modeled on hippocampal engram formation, in which eligible neurons compete for allocation to a memory trace based on intrinsic excitability, with the winners determining whether engrams overlap into integrated memories or stay separate. Optogenetic work in the Tonegawa lab shows that such engram ensembles form almost immediately across hippocampus, amygdala, and prefrontal cortex, link into a distributed "engram complex" through synaptic plasticity and dendritic-spine formation, and can be reactivated to recall the associated memory even when naturally silent. Tonegawa and Josselyn describe this same complex as the basic multiscale unit of memory, arising from excited local ensembles stitched together across regions by synaptic plasticity. Single-neuron recordings from the human hippocampus confirm that only a small, stimulus-specific fraction of neurons responds strongly to a given repeated item while the remaining population reduces firing, direct evidence for the sparse, distributed engram coding this module is meant to emulate. In the proposed model this sparse, competitively allocated population is implemented as an attractor network: exemplar-specific activity patterns become stable low-energy fixed points, so a partial or noisy cue converges through asynchronous updates onto the nearest stored pattern, exactly as demonstrated in Hopfield-style associative memories trained with a Hebbian rule. Point-attractor dynamics of this kind have been used explicitly to model associative memory, pattern completion, and classification, since each attractor can represent one category exemplar and its basin of attraction captures degraded or partial versions of it. The two modules are coupled the way hippocampus and neocortex are coupled in complementary learning systems models: a "notebook" network encodes each training exemplar by associating current cortical activity with a sparse, randomly assigned index pattern through Hebbian plasticity, its recurrent dynamics implement pattern completion so a partial cue can reactivate the full stored index, and that reactivated index in turn drives slow, error-corrective gradient-descent learning in a cortex-like "student" network that extracts generalizable structure. Concretely, in the Engram-Predictive Coding Network a new input is used to probe the engram attractor as a partial cue, and if it settles into a stored fixed point, the completed pattern is injected as an added top-down expectation at the hierarchy's highest layer, biasing the predictive-coding hierarchy's generative model toward a specific class hypothesis in the same way the notebook's completed index reactivates cortical representations. This dual role of the hippocampal formation in both episodic storage and online predictive processing, potentially through a single unitary neural code, matches predictive-coding accounts arguing that memory and prediction share the same computational substrate, which is the theoretical justification for letting one attractor module feed priors directly into a predictive-coding classifier. During classification, the hierarchy performs its usual iterative inference, propagating prediction errors upward and predictions downward until the free energy at each layer is minimized, but this process is initialized or continuously biased by whatever pattern the engram module completes, so previously seen inputs are classified almost immediately by pattern completion while genuinely novel inputs rely more on the slower, error-minimizing generative inference. The class label is read out once the combined free energy of the hierarchy and the engram-injected prior settles to a minimum, giving graded confidence: a sharp, low-energy minimum in the attractor module corresponds to a confident, memory-supported classification, while a shallow minimum corresponds to a purely inferred, generalization-based classification. Learning proceeds on two time scales mirroring biological memory allocation and systems consolidation. Engram allocation happens in one or a few trials through excitability-gated Hebbian plasticity, immediately usable for classifying the exact exemplar seen, because Hebbian weight changes make a newly presented pattern an attractor of the network as soon as it is learned. The predictive-coding hierarchy's synapses, by contrast, change gradually through local, layer-wise error minimization equivalent to backpropagation, extracting features that generalize across many engrams rather than memorizing any single one. Systems consolidation in the proposed model is implemented as offline notebook reactivation providing training targets for the cortical student network, comparing the notebook-reactivated output against the student's own internal prediction to generate the error signal used for slow generalization learning, exactly as in the teacher-student-notebook framework this component is drawn from. Taken together, the architecture instantiates biological plausibility on several independent grounds supported by the retrieved evidence: local, non-backpropagated error signals for hierarchical inference and learning, competitive, excitability-based allocation for sparse memory formation, Hebbian plasticity for one-shot attractor storage, and a hippocampal-cortical division of labor between fast indexing and slow generalization. No single study in the retrieved evidence combines engram-allocation mechanisms and predictive coding into one trained classifier, so the architecture above is a synthesis of separately validated components from the engram and predictive-coding literatures. A direct empirical test of this combined system's classification accuracy and biological plausibility therefore remains an open question for future work.

Reverse Differentiation via Predictive Coding

Salvatori T

Song Y

Xu Z

Lukasiewicz T

Bogacz R

This paper proposes how networks of nerve cells in the brain could learn according to an efficient method called "error back-propagation". This method is widely used to teach artificial neural networks, but it is not clear if the brain could use it. Previous studies described how this method could be implemented by networks of nerve cells for simple computations, and this paper extends it to more complex tasks.

Scientific Abstract

Deep learning has redefined AI thanks to the rise of artificial neural networks, which are inspired by neuronal networks in the brain. Through the years, these interactions between AI and neuroscience have brought immense benefits to both fields, allowing neural networks to be used in a plethora of applications. Neural networks use an efficient implementation of reverse differentiation, called backpropagation (BP). This algorithm, however, is often criticized for its biological implausibility (e.g., lack of local update rules for the parameters). Therefore, biologically plausible learning methods that rely on predictive coding (PC), a framework for describing information processing in the brain, are increasingly studied. Recent works prove that these methods can approximate BP up to a certain margin on multilayer perceptrons (MLPs), and asymptotically on any other complex model, and that zerodivergence inference learning (Z-IL), a variant of PC, is able to exactly implement BP on MLPs. However, the recent literature shows also that there is no biologically plausible method yet that can exactly replicate the weight update of BP on complex models. To fill this gap, in this paper, we generalize (PC and) Z-IL by directly defining it on computational graphs, and show that it can perform exact reverse differentiation. What results is the first PC (and so biologically plausible) algorithm that is equivalent to BP in the way of updating parameters on any neural network, providing a bridge between the interdisciplinary research of neuroscience and deep learning. Furthermore, the above results in particular also immediately provide a novel local and parallel implementation of BP.

ANNs are good at inference problems. Biological Neural Networks (BNNs) are good at inference too. ANNs are built out of neurons. BNNs are built out of neurons too. It makes intuitive sense that ANNs and BNNs might be running similar algorithms.
There is just one problem: BNNs are physically incapable of running the backpropagation algorithm.
We do not know quite enough about biology to say it is impossible for BNNs to run the backpropagation algorithm. However, "a consensus has emerged that the brain cannot directly implement backprop, since to do so would require biologically implausible connection rules"[1].
The backpropagation algorithm has three steps.
Flow information forward through a network to compute a prediction.
Compute an error by comparing the prediction to a target value.
Flow the error backward through the network to update the weights.
The backpropagation algorithm requires information to flow forward and backward along the network. But biological neurons are one-directional. An action potential goes from the cell body down the axon to the axon terminals to another cell's dendrites. An axon potential never travels backward from a cell's terminals to its body.
Hebbian theory
Predictive coding is the idea that BNNs generate a mental model of their environment and then transmit only the information that deviates from this model. Predictive coding considers error and surprise to be the same thing. Hebbian theory is specific mathematical formulation of predictive coding.
Predictive coding is biologically plausible. It operates locally. There are no separate prediction and training phases which must be synchronized. Most importantly, it lets you train a neural network without sending axon potentials backwards.
Predictive coding is easier to implement in hardware. It is locally-defined; it parallelizes better than backpropagation; it continues to function when you cut its substrate in half. (Corpus callosotomy is used to treat epilepsy.) Digital computers break when you cut them in half. Predictive coding is something evolution could plausibly invent.
Unification
The paper Predictive Coding Approximates Backprop Along Arbitrary Computation Graphs[1:1] "demonstrate[s] that predictive coding converges asymptotically (and in practice rapidly) to exact backprop gradients on arbitrary computation graphs using only local learning rules." The authors have unified predictive coding and backpropagation into a single theory of neural networks. Predictive coding and backpropagation are separate hardware implementations of what is ultimately the same algorithm.
There are two big implications of this.
This paper permanently fuses artificial intelligence and neuroscience into a single mathematical field.
This paper opens up possibilities for neuromorphic computing hardware.

Abstract
Memories for events are thought to be represented in sparse, distributed neuronal ensembles (or engrams). In this article, we review how neurons are chosen to become part of a particular engram, via a process of neuronal allocation. Experiments in rodents indicate that eligible neurons compete for allocation to a given engram, with more excitable neurons winning this competition. In parallel with rodent studies, recent findings in humans verify the importance of this memory integration process for linking memories that occur close in time or share related content. A deeper understanding of allocation promises to provide insights into the logic underlying how knowledge is normally organized in the brain and the disorders in which this process has gone awry.

A biologically plausible classifier can be built by fusing two well-supported neural mechanisms: sparse, competitively allocated engram ensembles that store individual experiences, and hierarchical predictive-coding circuits that infer the causes of sensory input through iterative error minimization.
Call this architecture the Engram-Predictive Coding Network: a two-module system in which a fast, Hopfield-like engram store interacts with a slower, hierarchical generative-model classifier.

The classifier backbone follows the Rao-Ballard scheme, in which each layer holds an estimate of hidden causes r, top-down synaptic weights U encode a generative model predicting the layer below, and inference amounts to maximum-a-posteriori estimation of r from the prediction error between actual and predicted input.
Because this scheme uses purely local error signals rather than globally backpropagated derivatives, it satisfies the core biological constraint that action potentials do not travel backward along axons.
Salvatori et al. show that a predictive-coding variant, zero-divergence inference learning, generalizes to arbitrary computation graphs and reproduces the exact weight updates of backpropagation using only local, parallel rules, so the hierarchy's output layer can serve as a class-label readout without sacrificing biological realism.
A concrete instantiation trains multi-layer, cortex-like networks under Hebbian principles by comparing top-down feedback predictions against bottom-up sensory input to generate the error signal that drives both inference and learning.

The memory module is modeled on hippocampal engram formation, in which eligible neurons compete for allocation to a memory trace based on intrinsic excitability, with the winners determining whether engrams overlap into integrated memories or stay separate.
Optogenetic work in the Tonegawa lab shows that such engram ensembles form almost immediately across hippocampus, amygdala, and prefrontal cortex, link into a distributed "engram complex" through synaptic plasticity and dendritic-spine formation, and can be reactivated to recall the associated memory even when naturally silent.
Tonegawa and Josselyn describe this same complex as the basic multiscale unit of memory, arising from excited local ensembles stitched together across regions by synaptic plasticity.
In the proposed model this sparse, competitively allocated population is implemented as an attractor network: exemplar-specific activity patterns become stable fixed points of an energy function, so a partial or noisy cue converges through asynchronous updates to the nearest stored pattern, exactly as in Hopfield-style associative memories trained with a Hebbian rule.
Point-attractor dynamics of this kind have been used explicitly to model associative memory, pattern completion, and classification, since each attractor can represent one category exemplar and its basin of attraction captures degraded versions of it.
Rolls-style autoencoder implementations of hippocampal pattern separation and completion, orthogonalizing entorhinal input into a sparse dentate-gyrus-like code that CA3-like autoassociation later completes from partial cues, provide a biologically grounded circuit for this attractor module.

The two modules are coupled the way hippocampus and neocortex are coupled in complementary learning systems: the engram attractor acts as a fast "notebook" that one-shot encodes each training exemplar via Hebbian plasticity, while the predictive-coding hierarchy acts as a slow "student" that learns generalizable structure from the notebook's reactivations, with the amount of reactivation-driven consolidation regulated by how predictable those reactivations are, curbing overfitting to idiosyncratic exemplars.
Concretely, a new input is used to probe the engram attractor as a partial cue; if it settles into a stored fixed point, that completed pattern is injected as an added top-down expectation at the hierarchy's highest layer, functioning like a hippocampal index that biases the cortical generative model toward a specific class hypothesis.
This dual role of the hippocampal formation in both episodic storage and online predictive processing, potentially through a single unitary neural code, matches predictive-coding accounts arguing that memory and prediction share the same computational substrate.

During classification, the hierarchy performs iterative inference, propagating prediction errors upward and predictions downward until free energy at each layer is minimized, but this process is initialized or continuously biased by whatever pattern the engram module completes, so previously seen inputs are classified almost immediately while novel inputs rely more on slower generative inference.
The class label is read out once the combined free energy of the hierarchy and the engram-injected prior settles to a minimum, giving graded confidence: sharp minima correspond to confident, memory-supported classifications, and shallow minima correspond to purely inferred, generalization-based classifications.

Learning proceeds on two time scales mirroring biological memory allocation and systems consolidation: engram allocation happens in one or a few trials through excitability-gated Hebbian plasticity, immediately usable for classifying the exact exemplar seen, whereas the predictive-coding hierarchy's synapses change gradually through local, layer-wise error minimization equivalent to backpropagation, extracting features that generalize across many engrams.
Because unregulated transfer from the engram module to the hierarchy can cause overfitting to noise in individual exemplars, consolidation is gated to occur only when it measurably improves the hierarchy's generalization performance, a principle demonstrated mathematically in generalization-optimized complementary-learning-systems models built from a teacher-student-notebook framework.

No single study in the retrieved evidence combines engram-allocation mechanisms and predictive coding into one trained classifier; the architecture above synthesizes separately validated components from the engram and predictive-coding literatures.
A direct empirical test of this combined system's classification accuracy and biological plausibility therefore remains an open question for future work.

By characterizing mathematically the effect of changes to the activation of individual units on a property of the entire neural architecture called energy, Hopfield (1982) provided the important link between local interactions and global behaviour. In this chapter, we will explore the idea of energy and demonstrate how Hopfield architectures "descend on an energy surface". We start by providing an overview of the purpose of the Hopfield network. Then we outline the architecture including the threshold activation function, asynchronous updating and hebbian learning. Finally, we explain how a Hopfield network is able to store patterns of activity so that they can be reconstructed from partial or noisy cues.

Suppose we have a large plastic sheet that we want to lay as flat as possible on the ground. To lay our sheet we employ a cyclic procedure. Firstly, we find a low point on it. Then we build up that section by placing sand underneath it. Then we find another low point and build it up; continuing until we are satisfied that the sheet is flat enough. How might we go about finding the low points? One possibility would be to place a drop of mercury on the sheet and watch as it rolls down the sheet. The point where it stops is low (although possibly not the lowest on the entire sheet) and would be a good candidate for raising. The idea of the state of a system (position of the mercury) descending on an energy surface (the plastic sheet) is a recuring one in the field of neural networks - both for describing changes to activations as a consequence of cycling and changes to weights as a consequence of learning. Figure 1 shows a schematic of our plastic sheet. The low points are the attractors. The region within which the drop will fall to a given attractor is its basin of attraction and the paths taken by the drop are called trajectories.

Figure 1: Attractors, basins of attraction and trajectories.

The Hopfield network is designed to store a number of patterns so that they can be retrieved from noisy or partial cues (see chapter 2 for a description of some of the important properties of neural networks). It does this by creating an energy surface which has attractors representing each of the patterns. The noisy and partial cues are states of the system which are close to the attractors. As a Hopfield network cycles it slides from the noisy pattern down the energy surface into the closest attractor - representing the closest stored pattern. One of the more visually appealing demonstrations involves storing a set of images. The network can then be presented with either a portion of one of the images (partial cue) or an image degraded with noise (noisy cue) and through multiple iterations it will attempt to reconstruct one of the stored images.

Figure 2 shows the results of a Hopfield network which was trained on the Chipmunk and Bugs Bunny images on the left hand side and then presented with either a noisy cue (top) or a partial cue (bottom). The images on the right hand side have been reconstructed by the Hopfield network. Notice that even in the face of substantial degradation the network is able to reconstruct a very close approximation to the original image. The quality of the network's reconstruction depends on the similarity of the stored images and the number of images that are stored given the size of the network.

Figure 3: The "Noisy Two" pattern on a Hopfield Network.

neti = wijai

ai = sgn( wijai)

sgn(x) =

1 if x >= 0

-1 if x < 0

An attractor network contains a set of n nodes, which can be represented as vectors in a d-dimensional space where n>d. Over time, the network state tends toward one of a set of predefined states on a d-manifold; these are the attractors.

In attractor networks, an attractor (or attracting set) is a closed subset of states A toward which the system of nodes evolves. A stationary attractor is a state or sets of states where the global dynamics of the network stabilize. Cyclic attractors evolve the network toward a set of states in a limit cycle, which is repeatedly traversed. Chaotic attractors are non-repeating bounded attractors that are continuously traversed.

The network state space is the set of all possible node states. The attractor space is the set of nodes on the attractor.
Attractor networks are initialized based on the input pattern. The dimensionality of the input pattern may differ from the dimensionality of the network nodes. The trajectory of the network consists of the set of states along the evolution path as the network converges toward the attractor state. A biologically plausible classifier can be built by fusing two well-supported neural mechanisms: sparse, competitively allocated engram ensembles that store individual experiences, and hierarchical predictive-coding circuits that infer the causes of sensory input through iterative error minimization.
Call this architecture the Engram-Predictive Coding Network: a two-module system in which a fast, Hopfield-like engram store interacts with a slower, hierarchical generative-model classifier.

The classifier backbone follows the Rao-Ballard scheme, in which each layer holds an estimate of hidden causes r, top-down synaptic weights U encode a generative model predicting the layer below, and inference amounts to maximum-a-posteriori estimation of r from the prediction error between actual and predicted input.
Because this scheme uses purely local error signals rather than globally backpropagated derivatives, it satisfies the core biological constraint that action potentials do not travel backward along axons.
Salvatori et al. show that a predictive-coding variant, zero-divergence inference learning, generalizes to arbitrary computation graphs and reproduces the exact weight updates of backpropagation using only local, parallel rules, so the hierarchy's output layer can serve as a class-label readout without sacrificing biological realism.

The memory module is modeled on hippocampal engram formation, in which eligible neurons compete for allocation to a memory trace based on intrinsic excitability, with the winners determining whether engrams overlap into integrated memories or stay separate.
Optogenetic work in the Tonegawa lab shows that such engram ensembles form almost immediately across hippocampus, amygdala, and prefrontal cortex, link into a distributed "engram complex" through synaptic plasticity and dendritic-spine formation, and can be reactivated to recall the associated memory even when naturally silent.
Tonegawa and Josselyn describe this same complex as the basic multiscale unit of memory, arising from excited local ensembles stitched together across regions by synaptic plasticity.
Single-neuron recordings from the human hippocampus confirm that only a small, stimulus-specific fraction of neurons responds strongly to a given repeated item while the remaining population reduces firing, direct evidence for the sparse, distributed engram coding this module is meant to emulate.

In the proposed model this sparse, competitively allocated population is implemented as an attractor network: exemplar-specific activity patterns become stable low-energy fixed points, so a partial or noisy cue converges through asynchronous updates onto the nearest stored pattern, exactly as demonstrated in Hopfield-style associative memories trained with a Hebbian rule.
Point-attractor dynamics of this kind have been used explicitly to model associative memory, pattern completion, and classification, since each attractor can represent one category exemplar and its basin of attraction captures degraded or partial versions of it.

The two modules are coupled the way hippocampus and neocortex are coupled in complementary learning systems models: a "notebook" network encodes each training exemplar by associating current cortical activity with a sparse, randomly assigned index pattern through Hebbian plasticity, its recurrent dynamics implement pattern completion so a partial cue can reactivate the full stored index, and that reactivated index in turn drives slow, error-corrective gradient-descent learning in a cortex-like "student" network that extracts generalizable structure. [shard_01881_67189]
Concretely, in the Engram-Predictive Coding Network a new input is used to probe the engram attractor as a partial cue; if it settles into a stored fixed point, the completed pattern is injected as an added top-down expectation at the hierarchy's highest layer, biasing the predictive-coding hierarchy's generative model toward a specific class hypothesis in the same way the notebook's completed index reactivates cortical representations. [shard_01881_67189] [shard_00586_75637]
This dual role of the hippocampal formation in both episodic storage and online predictive processing, potentially through a single unitary neural code, matches predictive-coding accounts arguing that memory and prediction share the same computational substrate, which is the theoretical justification for letting one attractor module feed priors directly into a predictive-coding classifier.
[shard_04650_20530]

During classification, the hierarchy performs its usual iterative inference, propagating prediction errors upward and predictions downward until the free energy at each layer is minimized, but this process is initialized or continuously biased by whatever pattern the engram module completes, so previously seen inputs are classified almost immediately by pattern completion while genuinely novel inputs rely more on the slower, error-minimizing generative inference.
The class label is read out once the combined free energy of the hierarchy and the engram-injected prior settles to a minimum, giving graded confidence: a sharp, low-energy minimum in the attractor module corresponds to a confident, memory-supported classification, while a shallow minimum corresponds to a purely inferred, generalization-based classification. [shard_05009_55461] [shard_00890_2839]

Learning proceeds on two time scales mirroring biological memory allocation and systems consolidation.
Engram allocation happens in one or a few trials through excitability-gated Hebbian plasticity, immediately usable for classifying the exact exemplar seen, because Hebbian weight changes make a newly presented pattern an attractor of the network as soon as it is learned. [shard_00475_69127] [shard_00890_2839]
The predictive-coding hierarchy's synapses, by contrast, change gradually through local, layer-wise error minimization equivalent to backpropagation, extracting features that generalize across many engrams rather than memorizing any single one. [shard_03958_40426] [shard_02684_61999]
